title: The Teaching Hinterland
author: Shaun Allison
summary: Shaun Allison develops the concept of the 'teaching hinterland' -- the vast territory of unscripted, unobservable teacher behaviors that sit between official professional standards and actual student outcomes. The piece argues that formal teacher evaluation frameworks capture almost none of what matters: whether the teacher greets students by name at the door, whether they maintain a consistent and warm demeanor across the school week rather than just during observations, whether they notice the child who is slightly off and respond to it before it escalates, and whether their instructional relationships have the texture of genuine care rather than professional obligation. Allison draws on interviews with students who, when asked what made a particular teacher effective, never cite pedagogical techniques but instead describe relational qualities: 'she knew when I was having a bad day,' 'he never gave up on me,' 'she was the same on a Friday afternoon as on a Monday morning.' The piece is a sustained argument that teacher quality is substantially located in the hinterland and that evaluation frameworks that ignore it are measuring the wrong things.
points: * Formal teacher evaluation frameworks capture almost none of what students later identify as the source of a teacher's impact: the relational, consistent, attentive behaviors that constitute the 'teaching hinterland.' * Students' accounts of what made particular teachers effective focus almost exclusively on relational qualities -- consistency, genuine care, attentiveness to mood -- rather than pedagogical techniques or content mastery. * The hinterland includes: greeting students by name at the door, maintaining consistent demeanor across the school week (not just during observations), noticing early warning signs in individual students, and the texture of genuine rather than performed care. * A teacher who is excellent during formal observations but inconsistent, tired, or dismissive the rest of the time is delivering a fundamentally different experience from what the observation data suggest. * Allison's policy implication is that hiring, coaching, and retention decisions based primarily on observation data are selecting on the visible sliver of teacher quality while the invisible majority remains unmeasured.
quotes: I've been asking students what made their best teachers effective for twenty years. They never say 'her questioning technique was excellent' or 'he used retrieval practice at just the right frequency.' They say: 'she knew when I was having a bad day.' 'He remembered things I'd told him months earlier.' 'She was the same on a Friday afternoon as she was on a Monday morning.'

The hinterland is where most teaching happens. It's what happens between the moments your lesson plan specifies. It's the thirty seconds at the door before class. It's the look that says 'I see you're not okay today.' It's the email sent at 9pm because you remembered a student mentioned something difficult in passing.

Formal evaluation captures the visible surface of teaching -- the lesson plan, the questioning technique, the behavior management strategy. It almost entirely misses the hinterland. And the hinterland is where the relationship is built, and the relationship is where most learning happens.

A teacher who is excellent in observed lessons and adequate in everything else is not an excellent teacher. A teacher who is merely competent in observed lessons but consistently excellent in every hinterland behavior -- the greeting, the noticing, the follow-up, the steady presence -- is doing more for students than the observation data will ever show.

We hire for the CV and the observation. We should be asking: is this a person who will be consistently present with students, not just occasionally brilliant in front of an evaluator? Those are related qualities but they are not the same quality, and we have built an entire profession around measuring the wrong one.
